sentences.label: Raising the risk
sentences.text: This part adds up six inputs with fixed weights: through it, each extra vessel coloured by fluoroscopy adds about the same, from about 26% at 0 to about 84% at 2 vessels for a typical patient, and higher cholesterol raises it steadily, from about 17% at 193 mg/dL to about 44% at 308 mg/dL.
A reversible defect on the thallium scan raises it to about 51% and a resting ECG other than normal to about 30%.

sentences.label: Lowering the risk
sentences.text: Being a woman lowers it to about 3% and fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL to about 12%.

sentences.label: Rare results
sentences.text: A thallium result coded 4 raises it to about 79% and a fixed defect on the thallium scan lowers it to about 15% (the model has little data on this, n = 2 and 15).

This part adds up maximum heart rate, chest pain on exercise and the ST segment with an ST depression step and a normal-response score; through it, a flat ST segment raises a typical patient's risk from about 26% to about 42%, chest pain on exercise to about 38% and typical angina to about 39%.

A higher maximum heart rate lowers it in an uneven way, from about 31% at 118 to about 23% at 175 beats per minute, and older age raises it in an uneven way, from about 12% at 42 to about 41% at 66 years.
Through its step, ST depression on exercise adds to the risk only once it rises above about 0.4 mm, slowly at first, then faster: for a typical patient from about 20% at 0 mm to about 70% at 2.8 mm.

Its normal-response score works the other way, so across the whole model more ST depression raises the risk with a flat ST segment, in an uneven way, from about 75% to about 94%, but lowers it otherwise, from about 38% to about 27%, flattening out near the top because the predicted risk cannot go much higher.

This part sets the risk by chest pain type, with an atypical-angina gate that also reads sex, vessels, the ST segment and the thallium scan: through it, typical angina takes a typical patient's predicted risk from about 26% to about 4% and non-anginal chest pain to about 7%.
For atypical angina, a marker and the gate pull in opposite directions: through the marker it lowers the risk from about 26% to about 12%, and through the gate it raises it to about 37%.

Across the whole model, more vessels raise the risk more with atypical angina, each extra vessel adding about the same, from about 7% to about 75%, against about 26% to about 84% without chest pain symptoms.
A downsloping ST segment also raises it more with atypical angina, from about 7% to about 57%, against about 26% to about 54% without chest pain symptoms (the model has little data on this, n = 17).

This part reads resting blood pressure and the ST segment: through it, higher blood pressure raises a typical patient's risk quickly at first, then levels off, from about 22% at 110 mm Hg to about 29% at 155 mm Hg, and a slope other than upsloping raises it from about 26% to about 54%.
Blood pressure counts much more without an upsloping ST segment, rising quickly at first, then levelling off: from about 37% to about 75%, against about 22% to about 29% with one.

Inside it, a saturation unit lowers the risk: nothing until about 131 mm Hg (between 112 and 131 mm Hg for different patients), then steadily, for a typical patient from about 54% at 110 mm Hg to about 6% at 155 mm Hg, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted risk cannot go much lower.
This part reads age: through it, the predicted risk is highest at about 60 years and lower either side, for a typical patient about 17% at 42 and about 12% at 66 years.

Inside it, an older-age step lowers the risk: nothing until about 60 years, then steadily, for a typical patient from about 26% to about 8%, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted risk cannot go much lower.
The step acts on 68 of 242 training patients, 38 of whom had heart disease; for its typical patient the predicted risk is about 98% without it and about 94% with it.

This part sets the risk by chest pain type, with an atypical-angina gate that also reads sex, vessels, the ST segment and the thallium scan: through it, typical angina takes a typical patient's predicted risk from about 26% to about 4% and non-anginal chest pain to about 7%.
For atypical angina, a marker and the gate pull in opposite directions: through the marker it lowers the risk from about 26% to about 12%, and through the gate it raises it to about 37%.

Across the whole model, more vessels raise the risk more with atypical angina, each extra vessel adding about the same, from about 7% to about 75%, against about 26% to about 84% without chest pain symptoms.

This part reads resting blood pressure and the ST segment: through it, higher blood pressure raises a typical patient's risk quickly at first, then levels off, from about 22% at 110 mm Hg to about 29% at 155 mm Hg, and a slope other than upsloping raises it from about 26% to about 54%.
Blood pressure counts much more without an upsloping ST segment, rising quickly at first, then levelling off: from about 37% to about 75%, against about 22% to about 29% with one.

Inside it, a saturation unit lowers the risk: nothing until about 131 mm Hg (between 112 and 131 mm Hg for different patients), then steadily, for a typical patient from about 54% at 110 mm Hg to about 6% at 155 mm Hg, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted risk cannot go much lower.
This part reads age: through it, the predicted risk is highest at about 60 years and lower either side, for a typical patient about 17% at 42 and about 12% at 66 years.

Inside it, an older-age step lowers the risk: nothing until about 60 years, then steadily, for a typical patient from about 26% to about 8%, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted risk cannot go much lower.
The step acts on 68 of 242 training patients, 38 of whom had heart disease; for its typical patient the predicted risk is about 98% without it and about 94% with it.
